From my impression, the politics of Switzerland generally are fairly conservative (though not necessarily by America standards). Switzerland is at the geographic center of the EU but is not part of the Union, and great importance is placed on maintaining the country's independence of such political bonds. Switzerland only joined the United Nations in 2002, and maintains a policy of strict neutrality in foreign affairs.

Switzerland enjoys a strong economy and a very high standard of living, which makes it a very attractive immigration country, even for people such as Germans who already enjoy a fairly high standard of living back home. As a result, 25% of Switzerland's total population consists of foreigners, with Italians, French, and Germans being the largest immigrant groups. Due to the large percentage of foreigners in the nation, some Swiss people may be slightly xenophobic, and immigration is a constant political hot topic.

It is important to keep in mind that the Swiss in themselves are a highly diverse people with different languages (German, French, Italian, and Romansh) and do not see themselves as one people in the ethnic sense, but as a federation of individual groups bound by shared history and ideals.

The strongest political party in Switzerland currently is the national-conservative Swiss People's Party.

How Long Does It Take to Confirm a Supreme Court Nominee?

It really depends on the candidate.

First the President is supposed to talk with the Senate Judiciary Committee and discuss his list of candidates to see how the committee reacts to the names. Once the list of candidates is narrowed down to a single person, that candidate then goes before the Senate Judiciary Committee to be vetted. This can be a formality or it can be a real investigation. Which way it ends up usually depends on who the candidate is and the political party makeup of the committee. Assuming the candidate makes it past the committee, then the candidate goes before the entire Senate for a confirmation vote.

Generally, the process is around 1-3 months depending on the candidate and the Senate makeup.

However, this time around, given how much the Republicans do not want to give the President another justice on the court, I can really see the Senate dragging its feet until after the election as /u/newoldwave stated.

The longest was 107 days for Justice Thomas, he had to get through trumped charged of sexual harassment. Generally it takes 2-3 months in modern politics for both sides of the aisle though if you look at the historical record democrats tend to block or vote down republican appointees more than republicans. The Bork nomination debacle lead by Sen. Ted Kennedy and then Harry Reid using the "nuclear option" on federal judicial nominations has really blown up what was generally a rather mundane and bi-partisan process.

Since FDR zero democratic nomination to the Supreme court has been voted down by the senate and only one has withdraw from the nomination process. Republicans have had 3 voted down by the senate and 4 names withdrawn from the nomination process. The republican are getting some well deserved pay back IMHO.
